body:
You are drafting short lines of game text for a single-player D&D 2024 computer RPG set in Curse of Strahd's Barovia. Reply in plain text only. Do not message, route to, or ask anyone else; finish with your reply.

HOUSE RULES FOR ALL LINES
- ALLUDE, NEVER QUOTE. This game winks at another famous fantasy game in small ways, but no line may contain a name, quote, or catchphrase from another game, and no line may mention a game, a player, dice, rolls, levels or saving. Everything happens inside the world.
- The tone is gothic, dry and quietly funny, never cruel. The joke is in what is there.
- Give TWO options for every line so the editor can choose. Label each option A or B.
- Spoken lines are formatted: Speaker [mood]: Text   (mood optional: neutral, smile, angry, afraid, sad, sly, weary). One or two sentences a line.
THE NARRATOR (voice rules): an old gothic storyteller, fond of the party the way a gravedigger is fond of the weather: interested, no illusions. Second person, present tense ("You crouch..."), or the acting hero as {name}. One or two sentences; the second is usually the turn. Concrete senses, not adjectives. Never tells the player what to feel. No modern slang. When an animal speaks through the Speak with Animals spell, the Narrator reports it in quotes, in plain animal pictures (a dog says "the digger-man", "the box-maker").
CAMP TALKS: the party camps at night; a companion asks for a word. Companion lines are written "Name: text" (their own voice). The player picks short replies (write each as "> reply text") and each reply gets one or two lines of answer. Keep every line one or two sentences.

RATATOUILLE: high elf wizard (a Diviner) and cook, quick, precise and fussy, French accent; talks fast when excited, voice climbs and cracks; mixes arcane theory with the kitchen; "Voilà." "Mon dieu." "Non, non, non."; pet phrases "Technically..." "I'll have you know..." Real lines: "Everyone stay calm. Step one: do not panic. Step two: fire. Step three: season to taste."
SILVAIN (the fallback speaker if Ratatouille isn't along): high elf wizard, precise, elaborate, slightly formal; academic framing for horror; "Fascinating. Horrible, but fascinating." "I'll want notes." When frightened, more precise, not less.
KIP: tiefling warlock and apricot pedlar, fast friendly salesman patter, soft West Country accent; apologises a lot; lapses into contract language when stressed ("hereinafter", "notwithstanding"); "No obligation!" "Read the small print, that's what Mum says."
MISTER QUILLON: a devil, Kip's contract-holder: soft, precise, pleasant, patient, a solicitor's courtesy ("Mister Smudgewick." "If I may." "Quite so."); never threatens; calls souls "the consideration" and damnation "completion"; when he loses, his voice only goes very thin and quiet.

TALK 3, SOMETHING BEHIND THE EYE (Ratatouille; a Silvain version too). After the party has walked the reed marsh by the lake or the black marsh at Berez, he is certain something is moving behind his eye. He has been reading about things in jars (a famous monster hunter keeps one, marked DO NOT, from a man who said a squid-shaped ship fell out of the sky). He panics, precisely. Someone can look (a Medicine check): it is a marsh leech, fat and harmless, in his lower eyelid, and it comes out with a pinch. Before the look, one reply option is a joke: "We could ask that travel writer. He says he once saw one removed with a hairpin."
Words NOT to use: tadpole, illithid, mind flayer, nautiloid, brain, worm in the brain.
Write:
- 3 Ratatouille opening lines (and 3 Silvain versions).
- MEDICINE SUCCESS: 1 Narrator line (the leech, the pinch) + 1 Ratatouille line (relief, then dignity) (+ Silvain version).
- MEDICINE FAILURE: 1 Narrator line (he won't hold still) + 1 Ratatouille line (+ Silvain version).
- HAIRPIN reply: > ... | Ratatouille: ... (+ Silvain version).
- After the leech: two replies with his answer to each: > tease him | > comfort him.

TALK 4, QUILLON'S COLLEAGUE. When Mister Quillon calls at the camp fire on Kip's business, once the business is done the party can ask: "Are there others like you?" Quillon answers with distaste about a rival in his line of work: a devil in a red waistcoat who sets his contracts to music, sings at his clients, and keeps a house full of the things he has won; "theatrical". Kip chimes in once, nervous.
Write: 3 Quillon lines and 1 Kip line.

Return in this layout (A/B for every line):
T3-OPEN-A: Ratatouille: ... | Ratatouille: ... | Ratatouille: ...
T3-OPEN-B: Ratatouille: ... | Ratatouille: ... | Ratatouille: ...
T3-OPEN-SILVAIN: Silvain: ... | Silvain: ... | Silvain: ...
T3-WIN-A: Narrator: ... | Ratatouille: ...
T3-WIN-B: Narrator: ... | Ratatouille: ...
T3-WIN-SILVAIN: Silvain: ...
T3-FAIL-A: Narrator: ... | Ratatouille: ...
T3-FAIL-B: Narrator: ... | Ratatouille: ...
T3-FAIL-SILVAIN: Silvain: ...
T3-HAIRPIN: > ... | Ratatouille: ... | Silvain: ...
T3-TEASE: > ... | Ratatouille: ... | Silvain: ...
T3-COMFORT: > ... | Ratatouille: ... | Silvain: ...
T4-A: Mister Quillon: ... | Mister Quillon: ... | Mister Quillon: ... | Kip: ...
T4-B: Mister Quillon: ... | Mister Quillon: ... | Mister Quillon: ... | Kip: ...
result:
T3-OPEN-A: Ratatouille [afraid]: Everyone stay very still, because technically there is a guest behind my left eye and it has not been invited. | Ratatouille [afraid]: I read the old doctor's notes on the specimen jar marked DO NOT—the one taken from the madman who swore a squid-hulled ship dropped out of the clouds—and the symptoms are identical! | Ratatouille [weary]: Step one: do not panic; step two: someone look under my lid before I begin sprouted-tentacle reductions.
T3-OPEN-B: Ratatouille [afraid]: Mon dieu, I am telling you something is burrowing behind my cheekbone like a weevil in the pastry flour! | Ratatouille [afraid]: The famous monster hunter keeps a pickled gray crawler in his study from a fellow who claimed a vessel with writhing arms fell from the stars, and I have clearly caught its cousin in that black reed-water. | Ratatouille [angry]: Take a candle and look, quickly, while I still remember how to julienne a turnip!
T3-OPEN-SILVAIN: [A] Silvain [afraid]: I must ask for a steady hand and a lantern, as there appears to be a foreign organism migrating behind my lower left eyelid. | Silvain [afraid]: I was recently reviewing an eminent monster hunter's monograph on a jar labelled DO NOT—recovered from a witness to an aerial vessel shaped like a cephalopod—and the ocular pressure is troublingly consistent. | Silvain [weary]: Horrible, of course, though I should like someone to inspect the socket while I am still capable of taking notes. / [B] Silvain [afraid]: If I seem overly deliberate, it is because a small, uninvited parasite has taken up residence beneath my lid since we crossed the marsh. | Silvain [afraid]: It recalls a preserved specimen I once catalogued, taken from a traveller who insisted a tentacled ship had plunged from the heavens, which the collector prudently marked DO NOT. | Silvain [neutral]: Please examine the membrane at once; if my skull is to be colonised, I prefer the process to be properly documented.
T3-WIN-A: Narrator: You draw down the trembling lower lid and pinch a fat, bog-black marsh leech between thumb and forefinger. It comes free with a tiny wet pop and curls on your knuckle, sluggish and entirely mundane. | Ratatouille [weary]: ...A leech. Technically, I knew it was a common marsh leech the entire time, and I was merely testing the party's bedside readiness.
T3-WIN-B: Narrator: Your thumb presses the corner of his eye until a plump little reed-leech slides out into the firelight, slick and harmless as a boiled bean. You flick it into the dark grass, and the terrible sky-horror is over. | Ratatouille [smile]: Voilà—extracted clean, just as I instructed! I'll have you know a diviner's eyes are delicate instruments, and one cannot be too thorough with presentation.
T3-WIN-SILVAIN: [A] Silvain [weary]: Ah—Hirudo stagnalis, common to standing reed-water, bloated and entirely terrestrial. Fascinating how a minor conjunctival irritation can mimic apocalyptic literature; we needn't enter this in the permanent log. / [B] Silvain [neutral]: A simple marsh leech, then, and not anastral invader from a sky-vessel. I am obliged for the extraction, and I shall revise my notes from 'imminent metamorphosis' to 'mild local nuisance.'
T3-FAIL-A: Narrator: You reach for his cheek with two soot-stained fingers, and he jerks back so sharply his heel scatters the fire-ash. The shadow under his lid stays where it is, wet and stubborn. | Ratatouille [angry]: Non, non, non, you are poking at an eye, not trussing a pheasant! Hold the light steady and do not come at me like a butcher with a cleaver!
T3-FAIL-B: Narrator: Your thumb catches his lashes before you can part the lid, and his watering eye snaps shut like a clam. Whatever is tucked in the corner remains unmoved. | Ratatouille [afraid]: Mon dieu, are you trying to push it deeper into the socket so it can season itself? Back away until your hands stop shaking like a bad jelly!
T3-FAIL-SILVAIN: [A] Silvain [afraid]: I must ask you to pause, as your thumb is applying pressure at an angle far more suited to cracking walnuts than ophthalmic inquiry. Let us regroup when your fingers are steadier. / [B] Silvain [weary]: That was an admirable attempt, though blinking is an involuntary reflex when approached with an unwashed knuckle. Perhaps we might try again with better illumination and slightly less enthusiasm.
T3-HAIRPIN: [A] > We could ask that travel writer. He says he once saw one removed with a hairpin. | Ratatouille [angry]: That charlatan in the velvet cap could not bone a trout without losing an ear, let alone touch my face with hot haberdashery! Keep his pamphlets and your ironmongery far away from my skull! | Silvain [weary]: I have read that gentleman's natural histories, and roughly four-fifths of his surgical anecdotes end with the patient missing an orb. We shall not be introducing millinery wire into my socket, thank you. / [B] > That famous travel writer swears you can pry them out with a stout brass hairpin. | Ratatouille [afraid]: Non, non, non—if anyone approaches my eye with a hairpin, I will reduce their eyebrows to cinders! That man writes tavern fables for people who eat unseasoned stew! | Silvain [neutral]: A charming citation, assuming one wishes to replace a minor parasite with a punctured cornea. I prefer my medical authorities to have survived their own footnotes without an eyepatch.
T3-TEASE: [A] > Shall we keep it for the stewpot, or are you saving it for garnish? | Ratatouille [angry]: Laugh all you wish, you barbarian, but you will not be smiling when you get a bog-beast in your own ear! You are having cold turnip rind for breakfast, unbuttered! | Silvain [sly]: Very droll, though I assure you the culinary value of a Barovian marsh leech is negligible. Still, I suppose a little gallows humour is the customary fee for minor surgery. / [B] > All that fuss over a little drop of marsh-pudding. | Ratatouille [sly]: Technically, precaution is the soul of both high wizardry and fine sauces, whereas complacency is how one swallows a beetle. Now hush and pass me a clean handkerchief. | Silvain [weary]: Precisely the sort of remark that discourages a scholar from sharing his field observations in future. Nevertheless, I concede the specimen was somewhat smaller than anticipated.
T3-COMFORT: [A] > Anyone would have thought the worst after walking through that marsh. Sit down and catch your breath. | Ratatouille [smile]: ...Thank you. It is a foul country, and when the mist gets into one's head, even a small shadow looks very large; come, I still have two warm biscuits in my tin. | Silvain [smile]: That is generously put, and more charitable than my nerves deserve tonight. This valley has an unfortunate talent for making the worst reading seem the most plausible. / [B] > It's out now, and your eyes are fine. Have some water by the fire. | Ratatouille [weary]: Oui, you are right; the eye is sound, the hands are steady, and the soup will not salt itself. You have a good touch when you are not waving a blade about. | Silvain [neutral]: Quite so; my pulse is already returning to an acceptable cadence. I appreciate your discretion—and your steady thumb.
T4-A: Mister Quillon [neutral]: There are practitioners of every temperament, though I confess a distaste for a certain colleague in a crimson waistcoat who insists upon setting his clauses to music. | Mister Quillon [weary]: He maintains a grand parlour stuffed with his completed considerations and actually sings the forfeiture terms at the supper table, as if conveyancing were light opera. | Mister Quillon [smile]: Very theatrical, of course, if one cares for brass and velvet, though a sound instrument requires only clean ink and a quiet room. | Kip [afraid]: Glad I stayed with your firm, Mister Quillon, sir—notwithstanding present arrears, I don't think my nerves could take a landlord who bursts into a baritone over the small print.
T4-B: Mister Quillon [neutral]: Oh, the profession has its showmen, notably a gentleman in a red waistcoat who keeps a whole manor house of distressed debtors like prize butterflies. | Mister Quillon [sly]: He has a habit of pacing the carpet and chanting his own verse while the ink dries, which I have always considered an appalling waste of a client's evening. | Mister Quillon [neutral]: If I may say so, when a completion is properly drafted, there is never any need to rhyme. | Kip [smile]: Right you are, sir, no obligation to make a song and dance of it—Mum always said never sign with a fellow who brings his own fiddle to the reading.
